claim: Mouse lifespan is particularly susceptible to endocrine or nutritional signals in the first few weeks of life, as tested by manipulations of litter size, growth hormone levels, or mutations with effects specifically on early-life growth rate.
source: Several previous lines of research have suggested, indirectly, that mouse lifespan is particularly susceptible to endocrine or nutritional signals in the first few weeks of life, as tested by manipulations of litter size, growth hormone levels, or mutations with effects specifically on early-life growth rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to previous research lines, indicating citation-based evidence, and draws from established scientific knowledge about early-life influences on lifespan.

claim: The pace of early development in mice can be influenced by exposure of nursing and weanling mice to olfactory cues.
source: The pace of early development in mice can also be influenced by exposure of nursing and weanling mice to olfactory cues.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about olfactory influences on mouse development.

claim: Odors of same-sex adult mice can in some circumstances delay maturation.
source: In particular, odors of same-sex adult mice can in some circumstances delay maturation.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about olfactory effects on maturation.

claim: The lifespan of female mice can be increased significantly by odors from adult females administered transiently from 3 days until 60 days of age.
source: we show here that the lifespan of female mice can be increased significantly by odors from adult females administered transiently, that is from 3 days until 60 days of age.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Female lifespan was not modified by male odors.
source: Female lifespan was not modified by male odors, nor was male lifespan susceptible to odors from adults of either sex.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing no effect of male odors on female lifespan.

claim: Male lifespan was not susceptible to odors from adults of either sex.
source: Female lifespan was not modified by male odors, nor was male lifespan susceptible to odors from adults of either sex.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing no effect of odors on male lifespan.

claim: Conditional deletion of the G protein Gαo in the olfactory system leads to impaired accessory olfactory system function and blunted reproductive priming responses to male odors in females.
source: Conditional deletion of the G protein Gαo in the olfactory system, which leads to impaired accessory olfactory system function and blunted reproductive priming responses to male odors in females, did not modify the effect of female odors on female lifespan.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Gαo deletion, likely from previous studies.

claim: Conditional deletion of Gαo in the olfactory system did not modify the effect of female odors on female lifespan.
source: Conditional deletion of the G protein Gαo in the olfactory system, which leads to impaired accessory olfactory system function and blunted reproductive priming responses to male odors in females, did not modify the effect of female odors on female lifespan.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing that the genetic manipulation did not affect the lifespan response to female odors.

claim: Very young mice are susceptible to influences that can have long-lasting effects on health maintenance in later life.
source: Our data provide support for the idea that very young mice are susceptible to influences that can have long-lasting effects on health maintenance in later life
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing early-life odor exposure affects later-life lifespan.

claim: The exceptionally long lifespan of Ames dwarf mice can be reduced back to that of non-mutant controls by transient exposure to daily GH injections started at 2 weeks of age and discontinued 6 weeks later.
source: Bartke's laboratory, for example, has shown that the exceptionally long lifespan of the Ames dwarf mice, in which longevity appears to reflect lower levels of growth hormone (GH) produced by the anterior pituitary, can be reduced back to that of non-mutant controls by transient exposure to daily GH injections started at 2 weeks of age and discontinued 6 weeks later (Panici et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Panici et al., 2010.

claim: Early-life GH injections block the development of multi-modal stress resistance shown by skin-derived fibroblasts of Ames dwarf mice.
source: Furthermore, these early-life GH injections block the development of multi-modal stress resistance shown by skin-derived fibroblasts of Ames dwarf mice (Panici et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Panici et al., 2010.

claim: Early-life GH injections prevent the lower levels of hypothalamic inflammatory characteristics of unmanipulated Ames mice.
source: and also prevent the lower levels of hypothalamic inflammatory characteristics of unmanipulated Ames mice (Sadagurski et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sadagurski et al., 2015b.

claim: Many characteristics of Ames dwarf mice plausibly connected to their longevity, insulin sensitivity, and cognitive health are blocked by early-life GH treatments when tested at 18 months of age.
source: Many other characteristics of Ames dwarf mice, plausibly connected to their longevity, insulin sensitivity (Dominici et al., 2002), and cognitive health (Kinney et al., 2001; Sun et al., 2005), are also blocked by early-life GH treatments when tested at 18 months of age, including changes in fat, muscle, plasma irisin and GPLD1, liver, and brain (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Dominici et al., 2002, Kinney et al., 2001, Sun et al., 2005, and Li et al., 2022.

claim: Lifespan can be increased in genetically normal mice by pre-weaning manipulation of litter size – mice weaned from litters in which litter size has been increased to 12 pups/nursing mother live longer than those in control litters of 8 pups.
source: Conversely, lifespan can be increased in genetically normal mice by pre-weaning manipulation of litter size – mice weaned from litters in which litter size has been increased to 12 pups/nursing mother live longer than those in control litters of 8 pups (Sun et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2009.

claim: Genetic selection experiments have shown extended lifespan in non-inbred stocks of mice that were selected for exceptionally slow growth in the first 10 days of life, or between 26 and 56 days of age.
source: Genetic selection experiments have also provided relevant data, by showing extended lifespan in non-inbred stocks of mice that were selected, for 17 or more generations, for exceptionally slow growth in the first 10 days of life, or between 26 and 56 days of age (Miller et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miller et al., 2000.

claim: Across strains of mice, age at sexual maturity correlates positively with median lifespan.
source: Across strains of mice, age at sexual maturity correlates positively with median lifespan (Yuan et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2012.

claim: Genetic manipulations that delay sexual maturity have been associated with longer lifespan in females.
source: and genetic manipulations that delay sexual maturity have been associated with longer lifespan in females (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Female mice that are exposed to male odors during development show hastened sexual maturity.
source: Female mice that are exposed to male odors (typically soiled bedding or male urine) during development show hastened sexual maturity (Drickamer, 1983; Vandenbergh, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Drickamer, 1983 and Vandenbergh, 1973.

claim: Exposing females to the odors of group-housed adult virgin females can delay sexual maturity.
source: In contrast, exposing females to the odors of group-housed adult virgin females can delay sexual maturity (Vandenbergh, 1973; Drickamer, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vandenbergh, 1973 and Drickamer, 1977.

claim: Exposure to females or their odors has been shown to be associated with increased masses of reproductive organs (testes, seminal vesicles) early in life in males, indicating earlier sexual maturity.
source: In males, exposure to females or their odors has been shown to be associated with increased masses of reproductive organs (testes, seminal vesicles) early in life, also indicating earlier sexual maturity in males (Vandenbergh, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vandenbergh, 1971.

claim: Hastened female sexual maturity was associated with an increase in mortality over the first 180 days of life and reduced litter sizes when breeding.
source: In one previous study, hastened female sexual maturity was associated with an increase in mortality over the first 180 days of life and reduced litter sizes when breeding, suggesting a cost to this developmental change (Drickamer, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Drickamer, 1988.

claim: The effects of odors on sexual maturity are initiated, at least partly, by detection of odorants through the vomeronasal organ.
source: The effects of odors on sexual maturity are initiated, at least partly, by detection of odorants through the vomeronasal organ, one of the two olfactory sub-systems in mice.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the olfactory system's role in sexual maturity.

claim: Female mice that have had their vomeronasal organ surgically removed do not show hastened sexual maturity in response to male odors.
source: Female mice that have had their vomeronasal organ surgically removed do not show hastened sexual maturity in response to male odors (Lomas and Keverne, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lomas and Keverne, 1982.

claim: Vomeronasal sensory neurons (VSNs) express hundreds of different sensory receptors, but these receptors largely use one of two different types of G protein for signal transduction.
source: Vomeronasal sensory neurons (VSNs) express hundreds of different sensory receptors, but these receptors largely use one of two different types of G protein for signal transduction (Munger et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Munger et al., 2009.

claim: The G protein Gαo is used for signal transduction in VSNs of the basal layer of the vomeronasal organ.
source: The G protein Gαo is used for signal transduction in VSNs of the basal layer of the vomeronasal organ.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about VSN signal transduction.

claim: Cre-mediated deletion of Gαo in the olfactory system has been shown to inhibit females from showing hastened sexual maturity in response to male odors.
source: Cre-mediated deletion of Gαo in the olfactory system has been shown to inhibit females from showing hastened sexual maturity in response to male odors (Oboti et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oboti et al., 2014.

claim: In female mice, FU led to an 8% increase in median lifespan compared to the ZU control group.
source: In female mice, FU led to an 8% increase in median lifespan, compared to the ZU control group
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: In female mice, FU led to a 9% increase in the age at 90th percentile compared to the ZU control group.
source: and a 9% increase in the age at 90th percentile.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: The log-rank test comparing all three treatment groups in females showed that treatment led to significant differences among the groups (p=0.04).
source: The log-rank test, comparing all three treatment groups, showed that treatment led to significant differences among the groups (p=0.04)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: For females, the FU mice were longer-lived than the ZU controls (p=0.01 by log-rank test).
source: and a follow-up test showed that for females the FU mice were longer-lived than the ZU controls (p=0.01 by log-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Male odors did not produce a lifespan change in female mice compared to controls (p=0.6).
source: Male odors did not produce a lifespan change in female mice compared to controls (p=0.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Treatment did not modify lifespan in the male mice (log-rank p=0.8 for all treatment groups taken together).
source: Treatment did not modify lifespan in the male mice; log-rank p=0.8 for all treatment groups taken together.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Cox regression analysis shows no significant interaction between genotype and odor treatment in either sex.
source: Cox regression analysis (see Table 2) shows no significant interaction between genotype and odor treatment in either sex.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Cox regression analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: The interaction term did not achieve significance in either sex, implying that the odor effect did not depend on genotype.
source: The interaction term did not achieve significance in either sex, implying that the odor effect did not depend on genotype.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical analysis results.

claim: There was no independent effect of genotype on survival.
source: In addition, there was no independent effect of genotype on survival.
evidence: This is a finding from the Cox regression analysis.

claim: Only the odor treatment had a significant effect on survival, and only in female mice (p=0.04).
source: Only the odor treatment had a significant effect on survival, and only in female mice (p=0.04)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Cox regression analysis.

claim: FU females lived longer than ZU females (p=0.015 without adjustment for multiple comparisons, and p=0.045 with Sidak adjustment).
source: The Cox regression calculation also confirmed the inference that FU females lived longer than ZU females (p=0.015 without adjustment for multiple comparisons, and p=0.045 with Sidak adjustment)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Cox regression analysis.

claim: No other pairwise comparison between treatment groups had a significant effect in either sex.
source: and that no other pairwise comparison between treatment groups had a significant effect in either sex.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Cox regression analysis.

claim: Within each genotype and sex individual comparison, there was no significant difference in survival between odor treatment groups using a log-rank test.
source: Within each genotype and sex individual comparison (e.g. WT females, mutant females, WT males, mutant males), there was no significant difference in survival between odor treatment groups using a log-rank test.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the log-rank test analysis.

claim: In females, the comparison of FU to control ZU mice produced a significance value of p=0.004 using the Wang and Allison method, showing that FU-treated females were more likely to reach old age than ZU-treated females.
source: In females, the comparison of FU to control ZU mice produced a significance value of p=0.004, showing that FU-treated females were more likely to reach old age than ZU-treated females.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Wang and Allison method analysis.

claim: None of the other paired comparisons reached significance in female mice using the Wang and Allison method.
source: None of the other paired comparisons reached significance in female mice
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Wang and Allison method analysis.

claim: None of the paired comparisons reached significance in male mice using the Wang and Allison method.
source: and none did so in male mice.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Wang and Allison method analysis.

claim: For female mice, exposure to female odors leads to a significantly higher body temperature at 22 months compared to the ZU control group (p=0.007).
source: For female mice, exposure to female odors leads to a significantly higher body temperature compared to the ZU control group (p=0.007).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional testing data at 22 months.

claim: There are no significant differences in body temperature between the MU group and FU mice or ZU controls in females.
source: There are no significant differences between the MU group and FU mice or ZU controls
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional testing data.

claim: There are no significant differences in body temperature among any of the groups for male mice.
source: and there are no significant differences among any of the groups for male mice.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional testing data.

claim: There were no effects of treatment on glucose levels in female mice at 12 months.
source: There were no effects of treatment in female mice
evidence: This is a statistical result from the glucose measurement data.

claim: Glucose levels were significantly lower in male ZU mice than in the FU or MU mice (p=0.004 for ANOVA, and p=0.01 for each pairwise comparison to ZU male mice).
source: but glucose levels were significantly lower in male ZU mice than in the FU or MU mice (Figure 2c; p=0.004 for ANOVA, and p=0.01 for each pairwise comparison to ZU male mice).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the glucose measurement data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There were no treatment effects, or significant interaction terms, for mean forepaw grip strength or for rotarod performance in either sex.
source: There were no treatment effects, or significant interaction terms, for mean forepaw grip strength or for rotarod performance (mean of three trials) in either sex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional testing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no significant differences in body weight at any age in female mice, except that ZU females were marginally heavier than mice in the MU or ZU control groups at 6 months of age (p=0.03, and p=0.04 if an MU mouse weighing 16 g is considered an outlier).
source: There were no significant differences at any age, except that in female mice, ZU females were marginally heavier than mice in the MU or ZU control groups at 6 months of age; p=0.03, and p=0.04 if an MU mouse weighing 16 g is considered an outlier.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the body weight trajectory data.

claim: The difference in body weight at 6 months in female mice is suspected to be a chance effect because these significance tests were not adjusted for multiple comparisons and because there were no large or significant effects in odor at any other age.
source: Because these significance tests were not adjusted for multiple comparisons and because there were no large or significant effects in odor at any other age, we suspect that this difference at 6 months is a chance effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on statistical considerations and the pattern of results.

claim: Body weight changes with odor treatment were uninfluenced by genotype.
source: Body weight changes with odor treatment were also uninfluenced by genotype
evidence: This is a finding from the body weight analysis.

claim: The genotypes of mice had similar body weights across the experiment.
source: and the genotypes of mice had similar body weights across the experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the body weight data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 'window of opportunity', or age at which a mouse is susceptible to early-life influences on late-life health, is not known and may differ depending on the specific form of environmental variation.
source: The 'window of opportunity', or age at which a mouse is susceptible to such influences, is not known, and may differ depending on the specific form of environmental variation
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the limits of current knowledge.

claim: GH treatments can prevent lifespan extension of Ames dwarf mice when initiated at 2 weeks of age, but fail in Snell dwarf and Ames dwarf animals when started at 4 weeks of age.
source: but it is noteworthy that GH treatments can prevent lifespan extension of Ames dwarf mice when these are initiated at 2 weeks of age, but fail in Snell dwarf (Vergara et al., 2004) and Ames dwarf animals (Bartke, unpublished results) when started at 4 weeks of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vergara et al., 2004 and unpublished results from Bartke.

claim: The basis for the transient susceptibility to factors that set the tempo of late-life decline is unknown, but seems likely to involve epigenetic modulation of events that are sensitive to nutritional and neuro-endocrine stimuli.
source: The basis for this transient susceptibility to factors that set the tempo of late-life decline is unknown, but seems likely to involve epigenetic modulation of events that are sensitive to nutritional and neuro-endocrine stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Fibroblast cultures from adult mice of the Ames and Snell dwarf mutant strains are resistant, in culture, to multiple forms of lethal injury.
source: Fibroblast cultures from adult mice of the Ames and Snell dwarf mutant strains are resistant, in culture, to multiple forms of lethal injury (Murakami et al., 2003; Salmon et al., 2005; Salmon et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murakami et al., 2003, Salmon et al., 2005, and Salmon et al., 2008.

claim: Fibroblast cultures from Ames mice subjected to early-life GH treatment are not resistant to multiple forms of lethal injury.
source: unless the Ames mice had been subjected to early-life GH treatment (Panici et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Panici et al., 2010.

claim: Fibroblasts derived from 1-week-old Snell dwarf and control mice do not differ in stress resistance.
source: In this context it is noteworthy that fibroblasts derived from 1-week-old Snell dwarf and control mice do not differ in stress resistance (Salmon et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Salmon et al., 2005.

claim: At 1 week of age, GH levels are still largely derived from the intra-uterine blood circulation, and are not yet controlled by the pituitary of the newborn mouse itself.
source: at this age GH levels are still largely derived from the intra-uterine blood circulation, and are not yet controlled by the pituitary of the newborn mouse itself.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about GH levels in newborn mice.

claim: GH exposure experience in the 2- to 8-week-old mouse modulates the hypothalamic inflammatory state in mice 18 months of age or older.
source: GH exposure experience in the 2- to 8-week-old mouse (Sadagurski et al., 2015b), as well as milk availability mediated by the size of the nursing litter (Sadagurski et al., 2015a), also modulates the hypothalamic inflammatory state in mice 18 months of age or older.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sadagurski et al., 2015b and Sadagurski et al., 2015a.

claim: Milk availability mediated by the size of the nursing litter modulates the hypothalamic inflammatory state in mice 18 months of age or older.
source: GH exposure experience in the 2- to 8-week-old mouse (Sadagurski et al., 2015b), as well as milk availability mediated by the size of the nursing litter (Sadagurski et al., 2015a), also modulates the hypothalamic inflammatory state in mice 18 months of age or older.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sadagurski et al., 2015a.

claim: Ames mice treated transiently with GH resemble WT controls in adipose tissue UCP1 levels, relative ratios of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory macrophages in adipose tissue, production of FNDC5 and its myokine cleavage product irisin by skeletal muscle, hepatic and plasma levels of GPLD1, and brain levels of protective factors BDNF and DCX.
source: Ames mice treated transiently with GH also resemble WT, that is, non-mutant, controls in adipose tissue UCP1 levels, relative ratios of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory macrophages in adipose tissue, production of FNDC5 and its myokine cleavage product irisin by skeletal muscle, hepatic and plasma levels of GPLD1, and brain levels of protective factors BDNF and DCX (Li et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2022.

claim: Early-life environmental factors can have long-lasting, presumably permanent, effects on many physiological properties of high relevance to health maintenance and disease resistance.
source: showing that these early-life environmental factors can have long-lasting, presumably permanent, effects on many physiological properties of high relevance to health maintenance and disease resistance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies about early-life GH treatment effects.

claim: Exposure to same-sex odor delays development in some circumstances.
source: We hypothesized that exposure to same-sex odor, which delays development in some circumstances (Drickamer, 1988; Drickamer, 1982), might also delay the rate of age-related decline
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Drickamer, 1988 and Drickamer, 1982.

claim: Female mice exposed early to odors from adult females had longer lifespan than females exposed to water.
source: and we found that indeed female mice exposed early to odors from adult females had longer lifespan than females exposed to water.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Male odor did not have an effect on female longevity.
source: Male odor did not have this effect on female longevity.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The FU-treated female mice resisted the age-related decline in core body temperature.
source: The FU-treated female mice also resisted the age-related decline in core body temperature
evidence: This is a finding from the functional testing data.

claim: There was no inter-group difference in grip strength or rotarod performance in FU-treated female mice.
source: although there was no inter-group difference in grip strength or rotarod performance, other indices of late-life physiological state.
evidence: This is a finding from the functional testing data.

claim: Male mice did not exhibit lifespan or performance effects in response to either same-sex or opposite-sex odors.
source: Male mice, in contrast, did not exhibit lifespan or performance effects in response to either same-sex or opposite-sex odors.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The genotype of the mice exposed to odor was not the same as the genotype (UM-HET3 genetically heterogeneous stock) from which urine and bedding was collected.
source: We should note that the genotype of the mice exposed to odor was not the same as the genotype (UM-HET3 genetically heterogeneous stock) from which urine and bedding was collected.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental design.

claim: Different mouse strains produce different olfactory signaling proteins.
source: because different mouse strains produce different olfactory signaling proteins (Cheetham et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cheetham et al., 2009.

claim: Different mouse strains express different olfactory receptors.
source: However, different mouse strains also express different olfactory receptors (Ibarra-Soria et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ibarra-Soria et al., 2017.

claim: VNO activation responses in mice to odors from the same or different strain of mouse has been reported as broadly similar.
source: although VNO activation responses in mice to odors from the same or different strain of mouse has been reported as broadly similar (Bansal et al., 2021; Silvotti et al., 2018).

claim: It's possible that different lifespan responses may occur if mice are exposed to odors from their background genotype.
source: In principle, it's possible that different lifespan responses may occur if mice are exposed to odors from their background genotype.

source: This G protein is important in mediating responses to peptide and protein-based ligands in basal VSNs (Chamero et al., 2011)

source: and has previously been shown to inhibit priming responses to male odors in females, including changes in sexual maturity (Oboti et al., 2014).

source: but does not affect normal body development or suckling behavior as has been observed with manipulations that impair main olfactory system function (Mandiyan et al., 2005).

source: Exposure of female mice to female odors has previously been shown to activate a different subset of VSNs compared to male odorants, including apical VSNs that use a different G protein in signal transduction (Silvotti et al., 2018).

source: Changes in sexual maturity with exposure to conspecific odors can be initiated even by brief exposure to the diluted urine of a conspecific after weaning

source: Exposure of flies and worms to food-based odorants, for example, limit the benefits of dietary restriction and influence measures of healthy aging, including sleep and daily activity patterns (Miller et al., 2022; Linford et al., 2015).

source: Some of these studies have focused on how perception of conspecific pheromones, detected through olfaction and gustation, can modulate Drosophila and C. elegans lifespan (Shi and Murphy, 2014; Maures et al., 2014; Gendron et al., 2014).

source: Worm perception impacts insulin-specific pathways
